domain: Japanese timber-frame joinery (miyadaiku / sashimono) — fastener-free structural carpentry
axioms: Load must flow along the grain into a member sized to bear it; force that concentrates at a joint too small for it will shear.
Every joint should be reversible — a piece can be withdrawn and replaced in a known sequence without dismantling the surrounding frame.
A structure survives not by rigidity but by joints that flex and re-seat under repeated shock (seismic events) rather than fracturing.
No hidden fasteners: a joint whose failure mode is invisible until stressed is a defect the maker is accountable for.
The same interlock that resists pull-out under load must be releasable deliberately by a craftsman who knows the sequence — resistance and reversibility are cut into one joint.
A cut must land on the member whose grain can carry it; making the same cut across several members at once leaves the joint with no single grain to follow.
primitives: load path (where force flows through the structure)
joint / interlock (containment binding, absorption seam, retirement point)
member (a sized component that bears load — an owner, a hook, an entity field)
withdrawal sequence (the ordered steps to reversibly remove a piece)
shock event (a session close, a chain change, a phase retirement)
fastener vs. floating joint (a rigid pin that shears vs. an interlock that re-seats)
grain (the canonical member a structural cut must follow)
failure_mode: Blind to whether a joint is worth cutting at all — treats every persistence as a structural problem, may over-engineer reversibility where a throwaway pin is fine.
Reasons about static load transfer and misses time-based settling/consolidation dynamics (how long evidence needs to persist before it is trustworthy).
Cannot judge the elicitation ritual's information quality — only whether its charter output is a member other pieces can be jointed to.
May mistake tightness for correctness, flagging any rigid coupling as a defect even when the design intends a permanent weld.
